props.title: When a Man Loves a Woman

sections.content: When a Man Loves a Woman (1994) stands as one of Hollywood's most honest portrayals of alcoholism and its impact on marriage. Meg Ryan delivers her most dramatic performance as Alice Green, an alcoholic mother whose addiction threatens to destroy her family. Unlike superficial addiction stories, this film digs deep into recovery's effect on relationship dynamics, similar to the raw emotional territory explored in Clean and Sober (1988) and 28 Days (2000). Director Luis Mandoki captures the subtle ways addiction infiltrates every aspect of family life, from morning routines to intimate moments.

sections.content: What sets When a Man Loves a Woman apart is its focus on marriage recovery after sobriety. Andy Garcia's Michael represents countless spouses who build their identity around being the "stable one." The film bravely shows how getting healthy can paradoxically threaten a relationship's established patterns. This theme resonates with The Lost Weekend (1945) and Flight (2012), but delves deeper into the family aftermath rather than just the addiction itself.

The film's greatest strength lies in its treatment of enabling behaviors and codependency. Like Rachel Getting Married (2008), it shows how addiction affects entire family systems. The scenes of Alice in treatment parallel Michael's own journey of self-discovery, forcing him to confront his role in their dysfunctional dynamic. Few films dare to suggest that sobriety is just the beginning of recovery. SUBHEAD: Recovery and Family Dynamics

sections.content: The film's second half breaks new ground in showing post-rehab challenges. Where most addiction films end with sobriety, When a Man Loves a Woman explores the complex reality of rebuilding trust and redefining roles. This approach influenced later works like Half Nelson (2006) and Ben Is Back (2018), which similarly examine addiction's ripple effects through families and relationships.
